name: 1 Timothy
author: The letter names Paul as its writer. He was a Jewish scholar trained as a Pharisee (a strict teacher of God's law), a tentmaker by trade, and a former persecutor of Christians who became a travelling missionary and founder of churches. Traditionally it is dated late in his life, perhaps in the early-to-mid 60s AD after a release from house arrest in Rome; many scholars instead think a later follower wrote it in Paul's name to pass on his teaching.
audience: It is addressed to Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and close friend of many years, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, whom Paul had left in Ephesus to guide the church there. The believers met in homes, and some teachers among them were spreading confusing ideas and stirring up arguments, so Timothy needed help organising leadership and church life.
era: Ephesus was a busy port and one of the largest cities in the Roman Empire, in what is now western Turkey, famous for its huge temple to the goddess Artemis. If Paul wrote the letter, Nero was emperor and Christians were a small, often misunderstood group; if it came later, it probably belongs to the late first or early second century AD. Society was built around households that included family members and slaves, and wealth and status mattered greatly in city life.

notes.1:3: Paul had urged Timothy to stay on in Ephesus while Paul travelled to Macedonia in northern Greece, a journey that does not fit neatly into the travels recorded in Acts.
notes.1:18: Paul names two men, Hymenaeus and Alexander, probably known to Timothy in Ephesus, whose faith had collapsed; a Hymenaeus is mentioned again in 2 Timothy.
notes.3:1: "Overseer" translates a Greek word for a local church leader; Acts describes Paul meeting the leaders of the Ephesus church earlier at the nearby port of Miletus.
notes.3:14: Paul writes hoping to visit Timothy soon, but sends these instructions in case he is delayed.
notes.4:1: This section answers teachers in Ephesus who were telling believers to avoid marriage and certain foods.
notes.4:11: Timothy was young by the standards of the day to be guiding older believers, and church leaders had earlier laid hands on him to commission him.
notes.5:3: With no state support, widows without family often faced poverty, and the Ephesus church kept a list of widows it supported.
notes.6:1: Some members of the church were slaves, and some of them served masters who were themselves believers.
notes.6:17: Ephesus was a wealthy trading city, and the church there included some well-off members.

flags.problem: In 4:1–5 the letter frames these teachings as a warning about what some people will do in later times. The note states as fact that it answers specific teachers already active in Ephesus. Many scholars read it that way, but stating it flatly overstates certainty.
flags.suggestion: Soften the wording, e.g. "This section warns against teachers, probably already active in Ephesus, who told believers to avoid marriage and certain foods."

flags.problem: "Laid hands on him" is church language an ordinary reader may not understand.
flags.suggestion: Add a brief explanation, e.g. "…had earlier laid hands on him (placing their hands on him while praying) to commission him."

unsure.problem: The flag notes that Hymenaeus and Alexander are named at 1:20, not 1:18, and raises moving the note's anchor to 1:20.
unsure.suggestion: Left unchanged. The note covers the whole passage 1:18–20, so a detail at 1:20 is correctly placed, and notes cannot be moved to another verse in any case. The wording does not read as if it were only about 1:18, so no rewording is needed. The flag also says a softer wording was applied, but no wording change is specified, so there is nothing to apply.
